title: How Smooth Waves Build Sharp Corners

scenes.purpose: Contrast smooth sine wave with sharp square wave
scenes.narration: A smooth sine wave curves gently everywhere, while a square wave snaps vertically. Can smooth curves *ever* build sharp corners?
Start with the fundamental sine wave, scaled by four over pi. It matches the *rhythm* of the square wave, but not its flat top.

scenes.purpose: Show the third harmonic as a separate mathematical object
scenes.narration: Now look at the third harmonic by itself: three times faster, and one-third as tall.

scenes.purpose: Demonstrate point-by-point addition of component waves
scenes.narration: Add them point by point. Where the third harmonic dips, it *flattens* the peak and steepens the sides.
Keep adding odd harmonics: five x and seven x. Each finite sum is still completely *smooth*, yet the walls grow steeper.
With fifteen nonzero odd terms—up to harmonic twenty-nine—the flat plateau locks in, hugging the square wave.
Zoom right into the corner. No matter how many terms we add, a *nine percent* Gibbs overshoot—eight point nine five percent—never disappears.

scenes.purpose: Connect Fourier analysis to real audio waveforms and frequency spectra
scenes.narration: That frequency recipe—breaking a wave into simple harmonics—is how synthesizers, equalizers, and audio tools shape *real* sound.
